title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
author: Patrick Lencioni
theme: Teams fail not for lack of talent or strategy but because of five linked behavioural problems, starting with a lack of trust, that leaders can learn to fix.
summary: Patrick Lencioni tells most of this book as a business fable. A struggling Silicon Valley technology company has talented people, money and a promising product, yet keeps falling behind. A new chief executive, Kathryn, concludes that the real problem is the senior team: capable individuals who do not behave as a team. Through a series of off-site meetings she patiently changes how they work together.
After the story, Lencioni sets out his model directly: five dysfunctions that build on each other like layers of a pyramid.
The base is an absence of trust. He means the willingness to be open about mistakes, weaknesses and the need for help. Without that, people guard themselves and waste energy on appearances.

Low trust leads to fear of conflict. Team members avoid honest, passionate debate about ideas and settle for polite, guarded discussion. Lencioni argues that productive conflict over issues, not personalities, is healthy and necessary.
Without real debate there is a lack of commitment. People who never voiced their views do not truly buy into decisions, even when they seem to agree. Clarity and buy-in matter more than consensus.

Weak commitment produces avoidance of accountability. If people are unsure what was agreed, they hesitate to challenge peers whose performance or behaviour hurts the team. The most effective pressure, he says, comes from colleagues rather than the boss.
At the top sits inattention to results. When accountability is missing, people put personal status, careers or their own departments ahead of the team's shared goals.

Lencioni offers practical tools for each layer, such as sharing personal backgrounds, discussing behavioural profiles, confirming decisions at the end of meetings and making results public. The leader must go first: showing vulnerability, encouraging debate, insisting on clarity and keeping everyone focused on collective outcomes.
Teamwork, he concludes, is rare not because it is complicated but because it demands discipline and courage.
takeaway: Build trust through openness, welcome honest debate, commit clearly, hold one another accountable, and put the team's results above personal interests.

questions.q: Which dysfunction forms the foundation of Lencioni's pyramid?
options: Inattention to results
Fear of conflict
Absence of trust
Lack of commitment
questions.why: The model starts with trust, because every other dysfunction grows out of people guarding themselves.

questions.q: What kind of trust does Lencioni say a team needs most?
options: Willingness to be open about weaknesses, mistakes and the need for help
Confidence that colleagues will meet deadlines
Belief that the leader always knows best
Faith that the company will avoid layoffs
questions.why: He focuses on vulnerability-based trust, where people stop protecting their image and admit their shortcomings.

questions.q: How does Lencioni view conflict within a team?
options: It should be avoided to keep morale high
It should be handled only by the leader in private
It is a sign the team has the wrong members
Productive debate over ideas is healthy and necessary
questions.why: He argues that honest, issue-focused debate leads to better decisions and stronger buy-in.

questions.q: Why do teams that avoid debate struggle with commitment?
options: Because decisions take too long
Because people who never aired their views do not truly buy into decisions
Because budgets are not approved
Because the leader refuses to decide
questions.why: Without having weighed in, members may appear to agree but do not really commit.

questions.q: According to the book, commitment requires:
options: Unanimous agreement from every member
Clarity and buy-in, even without full consensus
A formal vote on every issue
Approval from the board of directors
questions.why: Lencioni says people can commit to a decision they disagreed with if their views were heard and the decision is clear.

questions.q: Where does Lencioni say the most effective accountability comes from?
options: Annual performance reviews
Outside consultants
Written policies
Peers on the team
questions.why: He holds that pressure from respected colleagues is stronger and more immediate than pressure from the boss.

questions.q: What does 'inattention to results' mean in the model?
options: Putting personal status or one's own department ahead of the team's shared goals
Failing to measure sales accurately
Spending too much time on strategy
Ignoring customer complaints
questions.why: The top dysfunction is about members pursuing individual or departmental interests instead of collective outcomes.

questions.q: In what form is most of the book written?
options: An academic study with statistics
A collection of interviews with CEOs
A business fable about a leadership team
A step-by-step workbook
questions.why: Lencioni teaches the model mainly through a story about a new CEO rebuilding a dysfunctional executive team.

questions.q: Which practice does Lencioni suggest for strengthening commitment?
options: Avoiding written records of meetings
Letting each department set its own goals
Holding fewer meetings
Reviewing and confirming key decisions at the end of meetings
questions.why: Confirming what was decided ensures everyone leaves with the same understanding and can communicate it consistently.

questions.q: What is the leader's most important role in overcoming the dysfunctions?
options: Going first, by showing vulnerability and modelling the desired behaviours
Making every decision personally
Keeping disagreements out of meetings
Hiring only star performers
questions.why: The leader must model openness, encourage debate and keep the team focused on results for others to follow.
